introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2020. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain the terms: 'population problem' and 'underpopulation'.

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**'Population problem'.** A population problem exists when the size, structure or distribution of the population of a place is out of balance with its resources, technology and level of development, so that the standard of living is, or will be, lowered or the economic and social system is under strain. It may take the form of **overpopulation** (too many people for the available resources), **underpopulation** (too few people), a very high rate of natural growth, an ageing population or a very high dependency ratio, rapid urban growth, or an uneven distribution of the people. The idea depends on the **optimum population**, the number that makes the best use of the resources and gives the highest standard of living (the idea developed by Adam Smith, Dalton and others).

**'Underpopulation'.** This is the situation where the number of people in an area is **smaller than the optimum**, so that the resources are not fully used, given the technology available, and the standard of living could be raised if the population were larger. Typical signs are: unexploited or under-used minerals, land and forests; a shortage of labour and a small home market; high costs of infrastructure per head because the people are thinly scattered; a low output per square kilometre. The standard of living is not necessarily low, as in some well-off countries with plentiful resources and few people. **Examples:** parts of Canada and Australia, Siberia, and in Africa the thinly peopled forest areas of Gabon and the Congo Basin. An underpopulated area can usually improve its condition by in-migration, by encouraging births and by more investment.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Explain **two** reasons in each case why the following areas do not attract population concentration:

(i) high relief regions

(ii) hot desert areas

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Why some areas do not attract population concentration.** Dense population needs a reliable food and water supply, a tolerable climate, easy accessibility and the possibility of earning a living. Where these are missing, people are few.

(i) **High relief regions** (e.g. the Himalayas, the high Andes and the Rocky Mountains):
1. **Steep slopes and thin, stony soils** make farming difficult: the soil is easily eroded, mechanisation is impossible, and cultivation, house building, roads and services are costly. Landslides and avalanches are a hazard.
2. **A cold, harsh climate and inaccessibility.** Temperature falls with height, the growing season is short and frost and snow are frequent; the thin air is a physiological strain on people, and rugged terrain makes transport, markets, schools and hospitals hard to provide, so settlement is sparse. (Exceptions: tropical highlands with fertile volcanic soils and a cool, healthy climate, such as the Bamenda and Bamileke highlands, are densely settled.)

(ii) **Hot desert areas** (e.g. the Sahara, the Namib, the Arabian and Australian deserts):
1. **Aridity and scarcity of water.** Rainfall is very low and irregular, evaporation is very high, there is little surface water and groundwater is deep, so there is not enough water for drinking, farming or industry, and rain-fed agriculture is impossible.
2. **Extreme temperatures, poor soils and isolation.** Heat by day, cold at night, sandy, stony or saline soils, almost no vegetation, and great distances between settlements make farming unproductive and infrastructure very costly. (Exceptions: oases, irrigated valleys such as the Nile, and oil-producing areas, where people concentrate.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Briefly explain **three** factors that influence the shapes of population pyramid.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Factors that influence the shape of a population pyramid.** A pyramid is a graph showing the age-sex structure of a population, and its shape reflects the past and present balance between births, deaths and migration.

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_4_fig_1.png)

1. **Birth rate (fertility).** A high birth rate gives a **wide base** and a pyramid with a triangular shape (expanding population: e.g. Cameroon, Niger, many African countries). A falling birth rate narrows the base and produces a column or even a **contracting** shape with a narrow base (e.g. Japan and Germany). Family planning, education of women, age at marriage, economic conditions and cultural attitudes affect fertility.
2. **Death rate and life expectancy.** A high death rate, especially among infants and children, makes the sides **concave** and the pyramid narrow quickly with age; improved health care, nutrition and water supply reduce mortality and lengthen life, so the upper layers become wider (a broad top in the ageing populations of Europe and Japan). Epidemics (such as HIV/AIDS), famines and wars create notches or losses in particular age groups and in men.
3. **Migration.** In-migration of young adults (especially men seeking work, as in some oil-producing Gulf states and mining or plantation areas) causes **bulges** in the 20-40 age groups with an excess of males; out-migration from rural areas leaves the countryside with a **missing** young working group and an ageing structure, while it swells the towns.
